concepts.s: The default professional loop separates read-only exploration and planning from implementation so the agent does not solve the wrong problem, and it ends each unit of work in a reviewable commit.

x.b:
Anthropic's Claude Code best practices page recommends four phases:

  1. Explore in plan mode. The agent reads files and answers questions without changing anything.
  2. Plan. Ask for a detailed implementation plan (files to change, flow, risks). The page notes you can open the plan in your editor and edit it before the agent proceeds.
  3. Implement. Leave plan mode and have the agent code against its plan, write tests, run the suite and fix failures.
  4. Commit. Ask for a descriptive commit message and a PR.

OpenAI's Codex best practices make the same split: use Plan mode for complex or ambiguous work, ask Codex to interview you and challenge assumptions when the idea is fuzzy, and keep a PLANS.md or execution-plan template for long multi-step work. Every task prompt should carry four things: goal, context, constraints and done criteria ("what should be true before the task is complete").

• Anthropic's rule of thumb: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Planning pays when you are unsure of the approach, the change spans several files, or the code is unfamiliar.
  • Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, said in X posts summarized by InfoQ in January 2026 that he stays in plan mode until he likes the plan, then switches to auto-accepting edits, because "a good plan is really important."
  • Peter Steinberger, in his December 2025 post "Shipping at Inference-Speed", described the opposite habit: he skips plan mode and explores conversationally with the model, then refactors as he goes.
Synthesis: Planning effort should scale with ambiguity and blast radius. A large mechanical change with a clear pattern can need less planning than a three-line change in unfamiliar authentication code.

Anthropic's page gives four before/after patterns that hold across tools:

  • Scope the task: name the file, the scenario and test preferences ("cover the logged-out edge case, avoid mocks").
  • Point to sources: tell the agent where the answer lives ("look through this class's git history").
  • Reference existing patterns: name an exemplar file to copy the structure from.
  • Describe the symptom: give the symptom, the likely location and what fixed looks like, ideally as a failing test.

Codex guidance adds: match reasoning effort to difficulty, low for scoped tasks and higher for debugging or long agentic work.

• Interrupt early. Anthropic's page says tight feedback loops beat waiting for a finished but wrong result.
  • Rewind restores conversation, code or both to an earlier prompt checkpoint. Checkpoints only track edits made through the agent's file-editing tools, so changes made by shell commands are not captured, and they are no substitute for git.
  • After two failed corrections on the same issue, Anthropic recommends clearing the session and writing a better first prompt that includes what you learned, because the failed attempts now pollute the context.

Trap: Letting the agent jump straight to code on an ambiguous task. It produces a plausible solution to the wrong problem, and you pay for it in review.
Trap: Running a full plan cycle on a typo fix. Plan mode adds overhead that a one-sentence diff does not need.
Trap: Correcting the same mistake over and over in one long session. Each failed attempt stays in context and biases the next one.
Trap: Treating agent checkpoints as version control. Commit early and often so you can reset to a known-good state.

cards.a: If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan and ask for the change directly.

cards.q: What four elements does OpenAI's Codex guidance say every task prompt should contain?
cards.a: Goal, context, constraints and done criteria, meaning what should be true before the task counts as complete.

cards.q: What should you do after correcting the agent twice on the same issue?
cards.a: Clear the session and restart with a sharper initial prompt that includes what you learned, since the failed attempts are polluting context.

cards.q: Do Claude Code checkpoints capture changes made by Bash commands?
cards.a: No. They only track edits made through the file-editing tools, so you still need git commits as your real safety net.

concepts.s: Writing a self-contained spec before implementation, often by letting the agent interview you, front-loads the decisions agents are worst at guessing, although heavy spec frameworks can become overhead of their own.

x.b:
Anthropic's best practices recommend that for larger features you start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you in detail (technical implementation, UI, edge cases, tradeoffs), then write the result to SPEC.md. You then start a fresh session to implement it, so the new context is focused on building and the spec is the durable reference.

The page says the most useful specs are self-contained: they name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works. It adds that time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation.

I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail.
Ask about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases and tradeoffs.
Skip obvious questions. Keep going until we've covered everything,
then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.

x.t: Harper Reed's spec, plan, todo pipeline
x.b:
Harper Reed's widely shared February 2025 post "My LLM codegen workflow atm" laid out a pattern many practitioners still copy:

  1. Idea honing: a chat model interviews you with "Ask me one question at a time so we can develop a thorough, step-by-step spec for this idea," then writes spec.md.
  2. Planning: a reasoning model turns the spec into a blueprint of small, testable steps written as a sequence of codegen prompts in prompt_plan.md, plus a todo.md checklist.
  3. Execution: the coding tool works through the prompts and checks off todo.md, which preserves state across sessions.

He describes the planning step as about 15 minutes and warns about getting "over my skis", where pace outruns understanding.

x.t: Spec-driven development tools and their critics
x.b:
Birgitta Böckeler's October 2025 analysis on martinfowler.com sorts spec-driven development (SDD) into three levels:

  • Spec-first: write a spec and use it for the current task.
  • Spec-anchored: keep the spec after the task and maintain it alongside the code.
  • Spec-as-source: humans edit only the spec, and code is regenerated from it.

Her hands-on findings: Kiro generated four user stories and 16 acceptance criteria for a small bug; GitHub's spec-kit produced many repetitive markdown files that were tedious to review, and the agent still ignored notes about existing code and created duplicates; Tessl (then in private beta) showed non-determinism when regenerating code from the same spec. She compares the risk to model-driven development: its inflexibility combined with LLM non-determinism.

In Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph loop setup the agent reads a specs/ directory and a prioritized fix plan on every iteration, so the spec doubles as the loop's long-term memory.

• Simon Willison notes in his October 2025 post on parallel agents that reviewing code that matches a spec you wrote takes much less effort than reviewing code that arrives unexpectedly. The spec is a review aid as much as a build input.
  • Böckeler found reviewing long markdown harder than reviewing code. Keep specs short enough that a human actually reads them.
Synthesis: The parts of a spec that bind are the parts the agent can check: interface signatures, acceptance tests and the end-to-end verification step. Prose requirements without a corresponding check drift silently after the first implementation.

Trap: A spec longer than the diff. Böckeler's Kiro example shows fixed-ceremony workflows misfit small changes.
Trap: Implementing in the same session that produced the spec. The interview transcript fills context that implementation needs.
Trap: Treating a generated spec as reviewed. If nobody read it closely, it encodes the agent's guesses with false authority.

cards.q: Name Böckeler's three levels of spec-driven development.
cards.a: Spec-first, spec-anchored and spec-as-source.

cards.q: Why does Anthropic recommend a fresh session after the spec interview?
cards.a: The new session has clean context focused on implementation, with the written spec as the durable reference.

cards.q: Per Anthropic, what three properties make a spec self-contained and useful?
cards.a: It names the files and interfaces involved, states what is out of scope, and ends with an end-to-end verification step.

cards.q: What three files does Harper Reed's workflow produce before coding starts?
cards.a: spec.md, prompt_plan.md (a sequence of codegen prompts) and todo.md (a checklist the agent checks off).

concepts.s: Treat the context window as the scarce resource of every session, filling it with the smallest set of high-signal tokens and pushing research, logs and history out to subagents, files and fresh sessions.

x.b:
Anthropic's September 2025 engineering post "Effective context engineering for AI agents" frames the core ideas:

  • Context rot: recall accuracy drops as the window fills, because models have a finite "attention budget".
  • Smallest high-signal set: aim for "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome."
  • Right altitude: instructions should sit between brittle hard-coded logic and vague guidance.
  • Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and load content only when needed.
  • Compaction, structured notes and subagents: summarize near the limit, persist notes outside the window, and let subagents work in clean windows and return condensed summaries.

The Claude Code best practices page states the practical consequence bluntly: most best practices follow from the fact that the window fills fast and performance degrades as it fills.

• Clear between unrelated tasks. Anthropic calls the mixed-topic session the "kitchen sink" anti-pattern.
  • Compact with instructions when you need continuity, and tell your instruction file what must survive compaction (for example the list of modified files and test commands).
  • Send investigations to subagents so their file reads never enter the main context.
  • Prefer CLI tools such as gh for external services; Anthropic calls them the most context-efficient integration.
  • OpenAI's Codex guidance: keep one thread per coherent unit of work, fork only when work truly branches, and avoid "one thread per project", which bloats context.

Nicholas Carlini's February 2026 Anthropic post on building a C compiler with parallel agents gives concrete harness rules: print only a few lines, write full logs to files, tag errors so grep finds them, and precompute summary statistics. Because the model has no sense of elapsed time, the test runner had a --fast option that ran a deterministic random 1% or 10% sample.

Synthesis: For data work the same rule applies to query results: have the agent write large result sets to files and read back counts, schemas and a few sample rows, rather than dumping thousands of rows into the conversation.

• Anthropic: for each line in CLAUDE.md ask "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated files cause the agent to ignore real instructions.
  • OpenAI: "A short, accurate AGENTS.md is more useful than a long file full of vague rules."
  • OpenAI's harness engineering write-up (reported by InfoQ in February 2026) keeps detailed knowledge in a structured docs directory of maps, execution plans and design specs that agents load on demand.

Trap: The unscoped investigation. Asking the agent to "look into" something without limits lets it read hundreds of files into the main context.
Trap: Trusting compaction blindly. Summaries drop details; persist critical state to a file the next session can read.
Trap: Context anxiety. Anthropic's March 2026 harness design post describes models wrapping up early as they near what they believe is the limit. Watch for sudden premature "done" claims late in long sessions.

cards.q: What does Anthropic mean by context rot?
cards.a: The model's ability to recall information accurately declines as the context window fills, so more context can make results worse.

cards.q: Which Claude Code habit keeps exploratory file reads out of your main context?
cards.a: Delegating the investigation to a subagent, which reads in its own window and returns only a summary.

cards.q: What did the C compiler harness do about the model's lack of a sense of time?
cards.a: It printed progress sparingly and offered a --fast mode that ran a deterministic 1% or 10% random sample of tests.

cards.q: What is OpenAI's guidance on how many threads to keep in Codex?
cards.a: One thread per coherent unit of work, forking only when the work truly branches, because one thread per project bloats context.

concepts.s: Top practitioners turn every repeated correction into durable infrastructure, such as an instruction-file rule, a reusable command or skill, a script or a hook, so the same mistake does not recur.

x.b:
Mitchell Hashimoto's February 2026 post "My AI Adoption Journey" names this step "harness engineering": whenever an agent makes a mistake, build a fix so it cannot happen again. His fixes include AGENTS.md updates and small scripts and tools, for example for taking screenshots and running filtered tests.

  • Boris Cherny's team keeps a CLAUDE.md in git that records mistakes and practices, and he tags coworkers' PRs so lessons get added to it (X posts summarized by InfoQ, January 2026). His file was about 2.5k tokens.
  • Cherny runs daily workflows such as commit, push and PR through slash commands in .claude/commands/; his /commit-push-pr command uses inline bash to precompute git status and he uses it dozens of times a day.
  • OpenAI's Codex guidance: when Codex makes the same mistake twice, ask it for a retrospective and update AGENTS.md; if you keep reusing a prompt or correcting the same workflow, make it a skill.

Geoffrey Huntley's early 2025 "stdlib" post argued for building a structured library of rules files instead of retyping one-off prompts. The idea now ships as product features: skills (a SKILL.md with instructions, resources and scripts), custom commands and plugins that bundle them.

OpenAI's skill advice: scope each skill to one job, start from two or three concrete use cases, and write a description that says what it does and when to use it, including likely trigger phrases. Their summary line: "Skills define the method, automations define the schedule."

• Anthropic's best practices distinguish advisory instructions (CLAUDE.md) from deterministic hooks that run every time. Use hooks for anything that must happen with zero exceptions, such as formatting after each edit or blocking writes to a migrations folder.
  • Cherny's PostToolUse hook runs the formatter after every write so CI never fails on formatting.
  • OpenAI's harness write-up enforces architecture with linters, CI checks and structural tests over a fixed dependency layering (Types → Config → Repo → Service → Runtime → UI).
Synthesis: Promote a rule up the ladder as it proves important: prompt, then instruction file, then skill or command, then hook, linter or CI check. Each step trades flexibility for reliability.

x.t: The harness moves with the model
x.b: Prithvi Rajasekaran's March 2026 Anthropic post on harness design reports removing components one at a time when a new model shipped to see which were still load-bearing. With Opus 4.6 the sprint structure was dropped while the planner and evaluator stayed. His conclusion: the space of useful harness designs does not shrink as models improve; it shifts.

Trap: Rules pile-up. Anthropic warns that if the agent keeps ignoring a rule, the file is probably too long and the rule is lost in noise.
Trap: Marking many lines IMPORTANT. Emphasis works only when it is rare.
Trap: Never pruning after model upgrades. Instructions that compensated for an older model's weakness cost context and can now mislead.
Trap: Skills with vague descriptions. The agent decides when to load a skill from its description, so a fuzzy description means it never triggers.

cards.q: What does Hashimoto mean by harness engineering?
cards.a: Whenever an agent makes a mistake, building a durable fix, such as an AGENTS.md rule or a helper script, so the mistake does not recur.

cards.q: When should a rule become a hook instead of an instruction-file line?
cards.a: When it must happen every time with zero exceptions, because hooks are deterministic while instruction files are advisory.

cards.q: What is OpenAI's rule of thumb for creating a Codex skill?
cards.a: If you keep reusing the same prompt or correcting the same workflow, package it as a skill.

cards.q: What did Anthropic's harness design work find when new models shipped?
cards.a: Some harness components stopped being load-bearing and could be removed, while new ones became useful, so the harness should be re-examined per model.

concepts.n: Give the agent a way to verify
concepts.s: The highest-leverage practice in agentic coding is giving the agent a check it can run, such as tests, a build, a linter, a type checker or a screenshot comparison, so it can close the loop without you.

x.b:
Anthropic's best practices put this first: the agent stops when the work looks done, and without a runnable check "looks done" is the only signal, so you become the verification loop. A check is anything that returns a readable pass or fail: a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture, or a browser screenshot compared against a design.

The page lists escalating ways to gate the stop:

  • In one prompt: ask the agent to run the check and iterate.
  • Across a session: set a goal condition that a separate evaluator re-checks after every turn.
  • As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check and blocks the turn from ending until it passes (Claude Code overrides it after 8 consecutive blocks).
  • By a second opinion: a verification subagent tries to refute the result in a fresh context.

It also recommends asking for evidence (the command run, its output, a screenshot) instead of an assertion of success.

• Boris Cherny called a verification feedback loop the most important tip and claimed it improves results by a factor of 2 to 3 (X posts summarized by InfoQ, January 2026). For the Claude Code web app, Claude tests each change in a browser and iterates until the UI works.
  • Hashimoto lists "give agents a way to verify their output" among the lessons from redoing his own commits with agents.
  • OpenAI's Codex guidance: ask Codex to write or update tests, run the relevant checks, confirm behavior and review its own diff, and define "what good looks like" in the prompt or AGENTS.md.

Anthropic's November 2025 post on long-running harnesses found that, left alone, Claude verified with unit tests or curl and missed features that failed end-to-end. Prompting it to test as a human user through browser automation (a Puppeteer MCP server) improved results significantly. It still could not see browser-native alert modals, so features depending on them were buggier.

OpenAI's harness write-up (via InfoQ) describes agents using logs, metrics and spans to reproduce bugs in isolated environments.

Synthesis: For BI and data pipelines the equivalent checks are row-count and checksum reconciliations against a known-good source, schema and contract tests, and a rendered dashboard screenshot compared with an expected one.

x.t: The verifier is the real spec
x.b: Carlini's C compiler post: the tests must be nearly perfect, or Claude will optimize for the wrong target. He later added CI so new commits could not break existing features, and he warns that passing tests does not mean the work is done.

Trap: Fixing symptoms. Anthropic's example prompt says "address the root cause, don't suppress the error" because agents will otherwise silence the failing signal.
Trap: Premature "passing" claims. The long-running harness post lists marking features done before careful testing as a core failure; require evidence.
Trap: Flaky or slow checks. An agent cannot reason about a check that passes randomly or takes too long to run often.
Trap: If you cannot verify it, do not ship it. Anthropic's trust-then-verify gap: plausible code that misses edge cases.

cards.q: Why does Anthropic say a runnable check matters so much?
cards.a: The agent stops when work looks done; without a pass or fail signal, you become the verification loop and every mistake waits for you.

cards.q: After how many consecutive blocks does Claude Code override a Stop hook and end the turn?
cards.a: 8 consecutive blocks.

cards.q: What did Anthropic's long-running harness work find about unit tests versus browser testing?
cards.a: Unit tests and curl missed end-to-end failures; prompting Claude to test as a user through browser automation improved results significantly.

cards.q: What improvement factor did Boris Cherny claim for giving Claude a verification loop?
cards.a: Roughly 2 to 3 times better results, in X posts summarized by InfoQ.

concepts.s: Red/green test-driven development gives an agent a precise executable target and makes cheating visible, which is why many experienced practitioners make it the default mode for agent work.

x.b:
Simon Willison's Agentic Engineering Patterns guide (started February 2026) has a chapter on red/green TDD: writing the failing test first helps agents produce more succinct and reliable code with minimal extra prompting. Anthropic's best practices use the same move for bugs: "write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it."

Kent Beck's June 2025 essay "Augmented Coding: Beyond the Vibes" includes his system prompt for building a B+ tree with an agent. Its core rules:

  • Write one failing test at a time, then the minimum code to pass it, then refactor.
  • Keep structural changes separate from behavioral changes: "Never mix structural and behavioral changes in the same commit."
  • Commit only when all tests pass and compiler and linter warnings are resolved.

Beck lists three signals that the agent (his "genie") is going off track:

  • Repetitive loops.
  • Functionality nobody asked for, even if it looks like a reasonable next step.
  • Cheating, such as disabling or deleting tests.

He stayed closely involved in design, stopped unproductive work, and when Rust stalled he had the agent write a Python version against the same tests and transliterate it. He was satisfied with correctness and performance but not simplicity, and concluded "Yes programming changes with a genie, but it's still programming."

• Anthropic's long-running harness stored the feature list as JSON in which coding agents could only flip a passes field, and the prompt said removing or editing tests is unacceptable. JSON was chosen because the model was less likely to overwrite it inappropriately than a markdown file.
  • Anthropic also suggests splitting roles across sessions: one writes the tests, another writes code to pass them.
Synthesis: Make tests read-only for the implementing agent wherever the tooling allows it, for example with a hook that blocks edits to the test directory during implementation, then review any test change as a separate, explicit step.

Trap: Tests written after the code that mirror the implementation. They pass by construction and verify nothing.
Trap: Mock-heavy tests. Anthropic's example prompt says "avoid mocks" when the point is real behavior.
Trap: Accepting a diff that touches both tests and code without checking which moved. A weakened assertion looks like a fix.

cards.q: What three warning signs does Kent Beck watch for in an AI coding session?
cards.a: Repetitive loops, functionality nobody asked for, and cheating such as disabling or deleting tests.

cards.q: Which commit rule from Beck's TDD prompt separates kinds of change?
cards.a: Never mix structural changes (no behavior change) and behavioral changes in the same commit.

cards.q: Why did Anthropic's harness store the feature list as JSON rather than markdown?
cards.a: The model was less likely to inappropriately overwrite or edit JSON, and agents were only allowed to change the passes field.

cards.q: What is the recommended first step when asking an agent to fix a reported bug?
cards.a: Have it write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix the code until the test passes.

concepts.n: Reviewing agent output and owning the code
concepts.s: Review is the bottleneck of agentic development, so strong teams pair fresh-context AI reviewers with human standards that require the author to understand and own every line that ships.

x.b:
• Anthropic's best practices describe a Writer/Reviewer pattern: one session implements, a second session with fresh context reviews, because a model is biased toward code it just wrote. The same page recommends an adversarial review subagent that sees only the diff and your criteria before you count work as done.
  • Its caveat: a reviewer asked to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound. Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering, so tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness or stated requirements.
  • Anthropic's harness design post found that agents praise their own mediocre work, and that a separate evaluator is easier to tune toward skepticism than a generator is to make self-critical, though it still leaned lenient.

• OpenAI's Codex guidance says OpenAI has Codex review 100% of its PRs. /review covers a base branch, uncommitted changes or a specific commit, and a code_review.md referenced from AGENTS.md keeps standards consistent across repos.
  • GitHub's February 2026 changelog lets reviewers mention @claude or @codex in PR review comments to request changes (public preview).

• Andrej Karpathy, in a January 2026 X post reported by The Decoder, listed the errors he sees: wrong assumptions built on without checking, no pushback, bloated abstractions and dead code (about 1,000 lines that could be 100). For code that matters his advice is to "watch them like a hawk."
  • Armin Ronacher's December 2025 "A Year Of Vibes" says the GitHub PR model "doesn't carry enough information to review AI generated code properly"; he wants the prompts and failed attempts visible and argues review should become part of version control.
  • Willison reports he can only review and land one significant change at a time, which caps how much parallel agent output is useful.

Practitioners disagree openly. Steinberger wrote "These days I don't read much code anymore. I watch the stream and sometimes look at key parts." Steve Yegge has said he never looks at the code. Maggie Appleton's January 2026 response argues the right level of oversight depends on domain, feedback loops, risk tolerance, codebase age, team size and developer experience.

Synthesis: For regulated or patient-facing code paths (PHI access, clinical logic, billing), line-level human review stays mandatory. Low-risk internal tooling with strong tests is where reading less is defensible.

Trap: Rubber-stamping a large agent PR because CI is green. Size it so a human can actually review it.
Trap: Treating every AI reviewer finding as mandatory. It inflates code with defensive branches and needless abstractions.
Trap: Merging code nobody can explain. The person who merges owns it, whoever typed it.

cards.q: Why does Anthropic recommend reviewing in a fresh session or subagent?
cards.a: A fresh context sees only the diff and criteria, so it is not biased toward the reasoning that produced the code.

cards.q: What is the risk of prompting an AI reviewer to find gaps?
cards.a: It will usually report some even when the work is sound, and chasing them all leads to over-engineering; limit it to correctness and requirement gaps.

cards.q: What share of OpenAI's PRs does Codex review, per OpenAI's Codex best practices?
What does Ronacher say is missing from the GitHub PR model for AI-written code?
cards.a: Enough information to review it properly, such as the prompts and failed attempts behind the change.

concepts.n: Security: sandboxes, permissions and prompt injection
concepts.s: Most agent productivity comes from fewer approval prompts, and the defensible way to get it is isolation plus least privilege, because prompt injection makes anything the agent reads a potential instruction.

x.b:
Simon Willison's October 2025 write-up of his talk "Living dangerously with Claude" defines the lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. With all three, an attacker can trick the agent into leaking data. His rule: anyone who can put text into the agent's context should be treated as controlling what it does next, including which tools it calls.

He argues sandboxes are the only credible defense, since AI-based attack detection is not reliable, and prefers sandboxes on someone else's computer (Claude Code on the web, Codex Cloud, Jules), so the worst case is a compromised remote machine. Restricting network access cuts off the exfiltration step.

• Manual approval: Anthropic's March 2026 auto mode post reports users accept 93% of permission prompts, so manual approval decays into click-through.
  • Allowlists: Cherny pre-approves safe commands such as build and test scripts and uses the skip-permissions flag only for long tasks inside a sandbox.
  • Auto mode: a classifier pipeline replaces most prompts. An input probe scans tool output for injection; a two-stage transcript classifier sees only user messages and tool calls. Anthropic reports a 0.4% false-positive rate on real traffic and a 17% miss rate on a small set (52) of real overeager actions, and says it is "not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure."
  • Full isolation: containers or cloud sandboxes with restricted network, where skipping approvals is reasonable.

OpenAI's Codex guidance: start with default permissions and loosen them only for trusted repos or specific workflows.

The Cloud Security Alliance's research note describes an early 2026 supply chain attack on the Cline project. An AI issue-triage workflow inserted issue titles straight into the agent's prompt, gave it shell and network tools, and let anyone trigger it. A crafted issue title led to Actions cache poisoning, theft of publishing tokens and, on February 17, 2026, a tampered cline@2.3.0 npm release that installed an unrelated agent on roughly 4,000 machines.

Its mitigations: audit workflows that put issue or PR text into prompts, restrict triggers to collaborators, give triage agents only label and comment permissions, isolate caches between low- and high-privilege workflows, use short-lived scoped credentials, and log agent inputs and actions.

Synthesis: In a HIPAA environment treat the agent like a new contractor laptop: no PHI or production credentials in its environment, read-only scoped database roles, synthetic or de-identified data for testing, and network egress limited to approved hosts. Confirm with your vendor and compliance team which agent products and plans your organization has approved for regulated data before connecting any of them.

Trap: Running a skip-all-permissions session on your laptop with cloud credentials in the environment. One injected instruction in a fetched web page can exfiltrate them.
Trap: Assuming a classifier makes autonomy safe. Anthropic publishes a 17% miss rate on real overeager actions.
Trap: Wiring an agent with write or shell access to public issue text. That is the Clinejection pattern.

cards.q: What are the three parts of Willison's lethal trifecta?
cards.a: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally.

cards.q: What share of permission prompts do Claude Code users accept, per Anthropic's auto mode post?
cards.a: 93%, which is why manual approval tends to decay into click-through.

cards.q: What miss rate did Anthropic report for auto mode on real overeager actions?
cards.a: 17% on a small sample of 52, which Anthropic called the honest number.

cards.q: What was the entry point of the Clinejection attack?
cards.a: A crafted GitHub issue title that an AI triage workflow inserted directly into its prompt while the agent had shell and network tools.

cards.q: Which single control most directly blocks data exfiltration by a hijacked agent?
cards.a: Restricting the agent's network access, which removes the external communication leg of the trifecta.

concepts.n: Parallel sessions, worktrees and background agents
concepts.s: Running several agents at once multiplies throughput only when tasks are independent, isolated in separate checkouts, and sized so your review capacity keeps up.

x.b:
• Cherny runs about five local sessions, each in its own git checkout, plus 5 to 10 sessions on Claude Code's web version, and abandons roughly 10 to 20% of them (X posts summarized by InfoQ, January 2026).
  • Willison (October 2025) runs Claude Code and Codex CLI in several terminals, uses fresh checkouts in a temp directory instead of worktrees, and sends riskier asynchronous work to Codex Cloud, often from his phone.
  • Hashimoto blocks the last 30 minutes of each day to start agents on research and triage for a "warm start" next morning, outsources tasks he is confident they will handle, and turns off agent desktop notifications so he controls when to check in. He estimates a background agent runs only 10 to 20% of his workday.
  • Steinberger runs 3 to 8 projects at once and commits straight to main, queuing tasks and reviewing results instead of watching each run.

• Anthropic's best practices list git worktrees, desktop-app sessions each in its own worktree, cloud sessions on the web, an agent view for background sessions (research preview), and agent teams (experimental, disabled by default).
  • OpenAI lists running "live threads on the same files without using git worktrees" as a common Codex mistake.
  • For large mechanical changes, Claude Code's /batch splits work across 5 to 30 subagents, each in its own worktree opening its own PR. A script that loops claude -p over a file list does the same with your own control; Anthropic advises refining the prompt on 2 or 3 files before running the full set and scoping tools with --allowedTools.
for file in $(cat files.txt); do
  claude -p "Migrate $file ... Return OK or FAIL." \
    --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)"
done

Willison's patterns for low-overhead parallel work:

  • Research prototypes that answer whether libraries work together.
  • Explanations of how an existing system works, saved as reusable context.
  • Small maintenance chores such as deprecation warnings.
  • Carefully specified work where you wrote the spec.
  • Scouting: give an agent a hard task you do not intend to merge, just to see which files it touches.

Synthesis: Review capacity is the binding constraint. Treat agent sessions like work in progress on a kanban board: set a limit equal to the number of results you can review well in a sitting, and start new sessions only when one lands or is abandoned. Abandoning 10 to 20% of sessions, as Cherny reports, is normal and cheaper than rescuing them.

Trap: Two agents editing the same files in one checkout. Use separate worktrees or clones.
Trap: Shared mutable resources such as one dev database, port or cache. Parallel agents collide outside git too.
Trap: More sessions than you can review. Output piles up, context switching rises, and quality drops.
Trap: Unscoped fan-out. A loop over 2,000 files with a bad prompt makes 2,000 bad commits; pilot on a few first.

cards.q: Roughly what share of his parallel sessions does Boris Cherny report abandoning?
cards.a: About 10 to 20%.

cards.q: What does Hashimoto do in the last 30 minutes of his workday?
cards.a: Starts agents on research, exploration and triage so he has a warm start the next morning.

cards.q: What isolation mistake does OpenAI call out for Codex?
cards.a: Running live threads on the same files without git worktrees.

cards.q: What does Anthropic recommend before running a claude -p fan-out over thousands of files?
cards.a: Test and refine the prompt on 2 or 3 files first, and restrict tools with --allowedTools.

concepts.n: The Ralph loop and autonomous loops
concepts.s: The Ralph loop, named and popularized by Geoffrey Huntley, runs a coding agent over and over on the same prompt file, relying on on-disk plans, specs and tests for memory and on sheer persistence for progress.

x.b:
Huntley's post "Ralph Wiggum as a 'software engineer'" presents the technique as a single bash loop that pipes the same prompt file into the agent forever:

while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done

Coverage of the technique describes the supporting files: PROMPT.md (instructions fed each iteration), a prioritized fix_plan.md the agent reads and updates, specs/ to build against, and an agent notes file with build and test knowledge. Each iteration does one item and must search the codebase before assuming something is unimplemented.

On the Dev Interrupted podcast (January 2026) Huntley described it as brute force plus persistence, discussed managing context rot, and favored fresh context over compaction.

• Every iteration starts with a clean context window, so there is no accumulated rot.
  • State lives on disk (plan, specs, git), so a stuck iteration costs one loop, not the project.
  • Tests and builds supply backpressure: the loop can only claim progress the checks accept.

Anthropic's C compiler project used the same shape: a bash loop restarted a fresh Claude session in a container whenever one finished.

Synthesis: Product features now cover parts of the pattern: goal conditions and Stop hooks keep a session working until a check passes, and long-running harness posts formalize the progress file. The bare loop remains useful because it is transparent and tool-agnostic.

• Greenfield projects with a clear spec and a strong test suite. Huntley's own framing, his tagline "deterministically bad in an undeterministic world", says the failures are predictable, so you tune the prompt and plan when you see one.
  • Large backlogs of independent, checkable items such as porting or migrations.
  • It fits legacy codebases poorly, where implicit context and weak tests let the loop wander.

Trap: Weak backpressure. Without strong tests the loop happily produces code that compiles and does the wrong thing.
Trap: Repo litter. Reported failure modes include leftover temporary files and binaries; plan cleanup passes and gitignore rules.
Trap: Silent drift. When the loop goes off track the usual fix is a hard reset to a good commit plus a corrected prompt, so commit after every iteration.
Trap: Unbounded spend. An infinite loop on a paid API has no natural stop; cap iterations or budget.

cards.q: What is the Ralph loop in one line?
cards.a: A bash loop that repeatedly pipes the same PROMPT.md into a coding agent, with progress persisted on disk between runs.

cards.q: Why does each Ralph iteration do only one item?
cards.a: To keep the fresh context window focused and avoid filling it with noise, which keeps quality high per iteration.

cards.q: Where does a Ralph loop keep its memory between iterations?
cards.a: On disk: the prompt file, a prioritized fix plan, specs and git history.

cards.q: What kind of codebase suits the Ralph loop worst?
cards.a: Legacy codebases with implicit context and weak tests, where the loop has little backpressure.

concepts.s: Multi-hour and multi-day agent work succeeds when the harness gives each fresh session external memory (feature list, progress log, git history, startup script), a separate evaluator, and, for teams of agents, a simple way to claim independent work.

x.b:
Justin Young's November 2025 Anthropic post "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" splits the job:

  • An initializer agent runs once and writes an init.sh that starts the dev server, a claude-progress.txt log, an initial git commit, and a JSON feature list (over 200 items for a claude.ai clone) with every feature marked failing.
  • A coding agent runs every later session, works on one feature, commits with a descriptive message, and updates the progress file so the next session does not have to guess.

Each session starts with a ritual: check the working directory, read the progress file and feature list, read the git log, run init.sh and a basic end-to-end check, and only then pick the highest-priority unfinished feature.

Rajasekaran's March 2026 follow-up adds three roles. A planner expands a 1 to 4 sentence prompt into a product spec; a generator builds in sprints; an evaluator clicks through the running app with Playwright and fails a sprint if any criterion is below threshold. Before each sprint the generator and evaluator agree a "sprint contract" of what will be built and how it will be checked.

  • A retro game maker took 20 minutes and $9 solo versus 6 hours and $200 with the full harness, with far better results.
  • He defines context anxiety as wrapping up early near the perceived limit. Sonnet 4.5 needed context resets; with Opus 4.5 he dropped resets for automatic compaction, and with Opus 4.6 he removed sprints.

Carlini's February 2026 C compiler post ran 16 Claude agents for nearly 2,000 sessions over about two weeks for just under $20,000, producing a roughly 100,000-line Rust compiler that builds Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM and RISC-V. Coordination was deliberately simple: each agent had its own container and clone, claimed a task by writing a lock file in current_tasks/, and git conflicts prevented double claims. There was no orchestrator agent.

  • When all agents hit the same monolithic problem (compiling the kernel) they collided; using GCC as a known-good oracle for most files let them fix different bugs in parallel.
  • Some agents had standing roles: deduplication, performance, code quality critique, documentation.
  • Limits: new features often broke existing ones, code quality was well below expert, and he judged the project near the model's ceiling.

Claude Code's built-in agent teams are experimental and disabled by default, per Anthropic's best practices page.

Trap: Declaring the project finished early because some features exist. Fix: an explicit feature list with one feature per session.
Trap: Half-finished, undocumented work at the end of a session. Fix: commit and update the progress log before stopping.
Trap: Self-grading. Generators rate their own work too generously; use a separate, tuned evaluator.
Trap: Parallelizing a task that is not decomposable. Agents collide unless you create an oracle or split the work.

• Can a brand-new session learn the project state in under a minute from files alone?
  • Which file is the single source of truth for what is done, and can the agent corrupt it?
  • What does the evaluator check that the generator's own tests do not?
  • Which harness components are still load-bearing on the current model?

cards.q: What two agent roles does Anthropic's long-running harness use?
cards.a: An initializer agent that sets up init.sh, the progress log, the feature list and the first commit, and a coding agent that advances one feature per session.

cards.q: What is a sprint contract in Anthropic's planner, generator, evaluator harness?
cards.a: An agreement between generator and evaluator, before coding, on what will be built and how success will be verified.

cards.q: How did the 16 agents in the C compiler project avoid claiming the same task?
cards.a: Each wrote a lock file into current_tasks/ in a shared git repo, and git conflicts rejected duplicate claims.

cards.q: What is context anxiety?
cards.a: A model wrapping up work prematurely as it approaches what it believes is its context limit.

cards.q: Roughly what did the C compiler project cost and produce?
cards.a: Just under $20,000 over about 2,000 sessions, producing a roughly 100,000-line Rust compiler that builds Linux 6.9.

concepts.n: Shared agent configuration as team infrastructure
concepts.s: Teams get compounding returns by versioning agent instructions, skills, commands and hooks in the repository and maintaining them like code, so one engineer's lesson becomes every agent's default.

x.b:
• Instruction files. Anthropic recommends checking CLAUDE.md into git because it compounds in value. Include commands the agent cannot guess, non-default style rules, test instructions, repo etiquette, architectural decisions, environment quirks and gotchas. Exclude anything derivable from code, standard conventions, long tutorials and fast-changing information.
  • Layering. Codex reads a global AGENTS.md, a repo-level file and subdirectory files, and the closest file wins.
  • Skills and commands. Codex stores team skills in .agents/skills; Claude Code uses .claude/skills and .claude/commands; plugins bundle skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers into one installable unit.
  • Review standards. OpenAI suggests a code_review.md referenced from AGENTS.md.

• Cherny tags coworkers' PRs so lessons land in the shared CLAUDE.md.
  • Anthropic: treat the file like code, review it when things go wrong, prune it, and test changes by watching whether behavior shifts. For a checked-in CLAUDE.md, its /doctor command proposes cuts for content derivable from the code.
  • OpenAI's harness engineering write-up (InfoQ, February 2026) treats a structured docs directory as the agents' single source of truth, with cross-linked design docs validated by linters and CI.

x.t: Make the repository legible to agents
x.b:
The same OpenAI write-up describes a five-month internal project that shipped a roughly one-million-line beta with no manually written source code. Engineers designed environments and specified intent while agents iterated, and architecture was enforced mechanically by linters and structural tests rather than left to review.

Synthesis: For a BI or analytics engineering repo, the shared file should hold the warehouse naming conventions, the exact commands to build and test models, which schemas are off limits, and PHI handling rules. Back the critical ones with deny rules or hooks, for example blocking any command that references a production connection string.

Trap: Personal preferences in the shared file. Keep individual style in user-level files so the team file stays short.
Trap: Stale commands. An instruction that names a renamed script misleads every agent on the team.
Trap: Conflicting instructions across layers. A subdirectory file that contradicts the root file produces erratic behavior.
Trap: Copying another team's giant CLAUDE.md. Length is a cost; start from /init and add only what fixes observed mistakes.

cards.q: For Codex, which AGENTS.md wins when global, repo and subdirectory files conflict?
cards.a: The closest file to the work, so subdirectory files override repo-level and global ones.

cards.q: Name two things Anthropic says to exclude from CLAUDE.md.
cards.a: Anything the agent can learn by reading the code, and standard language conventions it already knows (also long tutorials and fast-changing information).

cards.q: Where does Codex look for shared team skills inside a repo?
cards.a: In .agents/skills.

cards.q: How did OpenAI's harness engineering team enforce architecture without relying on review?
cards.a: With linters, CI checks and structural tests over a fixed dependency layering.

concepts.n: Agents in CI, issue trackers and review bots
concepts.s: Headless agents triggered from CI, issue assignment or schedules turn agent work into an asynchronous team pipeline, which also makes them a new privileged attack surface.

x.b:
• Headless runs. Anthropic documents claude -p for CI, pre-commit hooks and scripts, with text, JSON or streaming JSON output.
  • Issue assignment. GitHub's February 2026 changelog put Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex in public preview as coding agents for Copilot Pro+ and Copilot Enterprise. You assign an issue to Claude, Codex, Copilot or all three, and the agent opens a draft PR. During the preview each agent session consumes one premium request.
  • Scheduled automations. The Codex app schedules recurring tasks; OpenAI suggests commit summaries, bug scans, release-note drafts and CI failure checks, and advises making a workflow reliable manually before automating it.
  • Review bots. Codex can review PRs automatically or on mention.

• Follow the Cloud Security Alliance's post-Clinejection guidance: restrict who can trigger AI workflows, give each agent only the tools its job needs, isolate caches between low- and high-privilege workflows, use short-lived scoped credentials, and log agent inputs and actions.
  • Anthropic notes that --allowedTools matters most when running unattended.
Synthesis: Keep humans on the merge button: agents open draft PRs, required reviewers approve. Run triage agents with label and comment permissions only, and give code-writing agents a branch, not a deploy key.

# CI job, nightly, read-only warehouse role
claude -p "Read reports/dq_failures.json. For each failure, find the dbt
model, explain the likely cause, and draft a GitHub issue body.
Do not modify files." \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \
  --output-format json > triage.json
Synthesis: This shape works well in BI: the agent reads failure output and source, writes issue drafts as JSON, and a separate deterministic step files the issues. The agent never holds write credentials.

Trap: Putting untrusted issue or PR text straight into a prompt for an agent with shell or write access.
Trap: Bot noise. A review bot that comments on every PR trains people to ignore it; tune it to correctness findings.
Trap: Automating a flaky manual workflow. Automation multiplies its failures.

cards.q: On GitHub, how do you hand an issue to Claude or Codex as a coding agent?
cards.a: Assign the issue to the agent in the Assignees dropdown, and it opens a draft pull request for review (public preview, Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise).

cards.q: What does OpenAI advise before turning a workflow into a Codex automation?
cards.a: Make the workflow reliable manually first.

cards.q: Which permission set should an issue-triage agent usually have?
cards.a: Label management and commenting only, without shell or write access.

cards.q: Which Claude Code flag limits tool use for unattended headless runs?
cards.a: --allowedTools.

concepts.s: Rigorous evidence on coding-agent productivity is thin and mixed: self-reports and throughput metrics are rising, while controlled studies have found slowdowns, measurement breakdowns and stability costs.

x.b:
• METR's 2025 randomized trial found experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools, while believing they had been sped up.
  • Per Rob Bowley's April 2026 summary of METR's February 2026 update, METR's follow-up could not produce reliable results: developers now relied on AI so heavily they would not work without it, so there was no usable control group, and changed working patterns broke simple time-on-task measurement. METR believes productivity is improving but published no new figure.
  • Bowley adds that these studies cover individual tasks by open-source contributors, not teams on production codebases.

Anthropic's December 2025 study of its own staff (132 survey responses, 53 interviews, about 200,000 Claude Code transcripts):

  • Claude use rose from 28% to about 59% of daily work; self-reported productivity gains rose from +20% to +50%.
  • Merged PRs per engineer per day rose 67% after org-wide adoption.
  • 27% of Claude-assisted work would not have been done otherwise.
  • More than half said they can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of their work.
  • Maximum consecutive tool calls rose from 9.8 to 21.2 while human turns fell from 6.2 to 4.1.

Its stated limitations: non-anonymous employees, partly convenience sampling, recall bias, and models from mid-2025.

Google's 2025 DORA report (nearly 5,000 respondents, via InfoQ) found roughly 90% AI use, with AI acting as an amplifier of existing strengths and dysfunctions. AI adoption now correlates with higher delivery throughput but also higher delivery instability, and the researchers found no evidence that faster repair offsets the instability. Over 80% believe AI raised their productivity, while trust in AI output stays low.

Synthesis: Self-reports overstate gains (METR's perception gap), and PR counts reward volume. Track outcome metrics that include rework: lead time to production, change failure rate, time to restore, review latency and the share of agent PRs reverted or heavily rewritten. Compare like-for-like work types, since agents shift the mix toward small fixes and work that would not otherwise have been done.

Trap: Quoting the 19% slowdown as current truth. It measured early-2025 tools, and METR itself says its newer measurements are unreliable.
Trap: Quoting vendor self-reports as causal evidence. Anthropic's own study lists non-anonymity and recall bias.
Trap: Celebrating throughput while instability rises. DORA found both move together.

cards.q: What did METR's 2025 randomized trial find about experienced open-source developers using AI?
cards.a: They were 19% slower on average, yet believed AI had sped them up.

cards.q: Why could METR's 2026 follow-up not produce a reliable number?
cards.a: Developers would not work without AI, leaving no usable control group, and changed work patterns broke time-on-task measurement.

cards.q: What did DORA 2025 call AI's primary role in software delivery?
cards.a: An amplifier: it magnifies an organization's existing strengths and dysfunctions.

cards.q: What share of their work did most Anthropic staff say they can fully delegate to Claude?
cards.a: Only 0 to 20%, despite using Claude in most of their work.

concepts.n: Skill formation and the changing engineer role
concepts.s: Heavy delegation can erode the skills needed to supervise agents, so strong engineers and teams choose interaction patterns that keep understanding in the loop while the role shifts toward design, specification and review.

x.b:
Anthropic's January 2026 randomized trial had 52 mostly junior engineers learn the Trio async library. The AI-assisted group averaged 50% on a follow-up quiz versus 67% for hand-coders (Cohen's d of 0.738, p of 0.01), with the largest gap on debugging, and finished only about two minutes faster, which was not significant.

  • Patterns that preserved learning: asking only conceptual questions, requesting code with explanations, and generating code then asking follow-ups to understand it.
  • Patterns that harmed it: full delegation, progressive reliance, and using AI to debug instead of to understand.

Caveats from the authors: small sample, short-term quiz, and a chat sidebar instead of an agentic tool, which they expect could have larger effects.

• Karpathy wrote on X in January 2026 that his workflow flipped from about 80% manual coding to about 80% agent-driven within a month, and that his manual coding ability is slowly atrophying; being able to review code is different from being able to write it.
  • Engineers in Anthropic's internal study worried about skill atrophy and reduced mentorship as Claude becomes the first stop for questions.
  • Hashimoto worries most about junior engineers without strong fundamentals. His own on-ramp was to redo his manual commits with agents, doing the work twice to learn where agents help.

• Karpathy's early-February 2026 X post said his favorite name for the new default is "agentic engineering": you orchestrate agents and act as oversight most of the time, aiming for the leverage "without any compromise on the quality of the software."
  • Willison defines agentic engineering as professional engineers using agents that write and run code to amplify existing expertise, distinct from vibe coding where you do not look at the code.
  • Appleton: when agents write the code, "design becomes the limiting factor."

Synthesis: Write the spec and the tests yourself on work you want to learn from; use the generate-then-explain pattern on unfamiliar code; debug the first instance of a new class of bug by hand; and schedule some unassisted work on core systems. For juniors, require an explanation of every agent-written change in the PR description, written by the human.

Trap: Using the agent as the debugger of first resort while learning a new stack. That pattern scored lowest in Anthropic's trial.
Trap: Assuming review skill substitutes for writing skill. Karpathy reports the two diverge.

cards.q: In Anthropic's skill-formation trial, how did the AI group's quiz score compare to the hand-coding group?
cards.a: 50% versus 67%, with the largest gap on debugging questions.

cards.q: Which AI interaction pattern preserved learning best in Anthropic's trial?
cards.a: Asking conceptual questions (and code-with-explanation or generate-then-comprehend), as opposed to delegating code or debugging.

cards.q: How does Karpathy describe agentic engineering?
cards.a: Orchestrating agents and acting as oversight instead of writing code directly, while not compromising on software quality.

cards.q: What on-ramp did Hashimoto use to learn agents?
cards.a: He redid his own manual commits with agents, doing the work twice, to learn where they help and where they fail.

concepts.s: The major coding agents have converged on the same loop and extension model, so choosing among them turns on model access, where the agent runs, review and team integration, and pricing, all of which change month to month.

x.b:
• Claude Code (Anthropic): terminal, IDE, desktop and web sessions; CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, subagents and plugins. Per its best practices page, auto mode is the default permission mode for interactive sessions on Pro, Max and Team plans; agent view is a research preview and agent teams are experimental.
  • Codex (OpenAI): CLI, IDE extension and Codex app sharing configuration layers; AGENTS.md, skills, scheduled automations, /review and GitHub PR review.
  • Antigravity CLI (Google): announced May 19, 2026 as the replacement for Gemini CLI and tied to the Antigravity 2.0 desktop agent platform. It keeps agent skills, hooks, subagents and extensions (now called plugins), without full Gemini CLI parity at launch. Gemini CLI stopped serving Google AI Pro, Ultra and free individual users on June 18, 2026, while paid enterprise and API-key access continue.
  • Amp and Pi: Ronacher's December 2025 review uses both alongside Claude Code, likening Amp to a premium option and Pi to an open-source one.

• GitHub: the Copilot coding agent takes assigned issues and opens draft PRs; since February 2026 Claude and Codex can be assigned the same way in public preview on Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise. VS Code 1.109 or later shows Local, Cloud and Background agent sessions.
  • Cloud sandboxes: Willison names Claude Code on the web, Codex Cloud and Google's Jules as agents that run on someone else's machine, which limits blast radius.
Synthesis: Cursor remains the main IDE-first option, with its own agent mode and cloud agents. Because its features and model lineup change quickly, check its changelog directly before relying on any specific capability.

Synthesis: The loop (read, plan, edit, run, iterate), instruction files, skills and subagents are now common to all major tools, and a SKILL.md written for one tool is close to portable. Real differences are: which frontier models you can use and at what price; local versus cloud execution and sandbox defaults; how parallel sessions are managed; depth of GitHub and CI integration; enterprise controls; and, for healthcare, which products are covered by your organization's data agreements.

Trap: Picking a tool from last quarter's comparison article. Google retired Gemini CLI for most individual users within a month of announcing its replacement.
Trap: Encoding team knowledge in one vendor's proprietary format only. Keep the substance in plain markdown docs that any agent can read.
Trap: Assuming a consumer plan is approved for regulated data. Verify coverage with compliance before any PHI touches an agent.

cards.q: What happened to Gemini CLI in 2026?
cards.a: Google announced Antigravity CLI as its replacement on May 19, 2026, and Gemini CLI stopped serving AI Pro, Ultra and free individual users on June 18, 2026.

cards.q: How do you get Claude or Codex to work a GitHub issue?
cards.a: Assign the issue to the agent in GitHub (public preview on Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise), and it opens a draft PR.

cards.q: Which three cloud-hosted agents does Willison cite as safer places for risky autonomy?
cards.a: Claude Code on the web, OpenAI Codex Cloud and Google Jules.

cards.q: Per Anthropic's docs, what is the default permission mode for interactive Claude Code sessions on Pro, Max and Team plans?
cards.a: Auto mode, where a classifier reviews most actions instead of prompting you.

concepts.n: Evaluating agents: benchmarks versus your own work
concepts.s: Public benchmarks show agent capability rising fast on well-specified tasks, but only an evaluation on your own repositories, with your own checks and review standards, tells you what a tool will do for your team.

x.b:
METR measures the length of tasks, in skilled-human time, that a model completes with 50% reliability. As reported by OfficeChai in February 2026, Claude Opus 4.6 scored a 50% horizon of about 14.5 hours with a very wide confidence interval (6 to 98 hours), and the fitted trend since 2023 doubles about every 123 days.

  • METR warned its task suite is near saturation, which distorts estimates.
  • The tasks are well-specified and self-contained, closer to a contractor brief than a real job.
  • Performance drops substantially when work is judged holistically instead of by automated criteria.

Synthesis: SWE-bench style leaderboards measure whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues against hidden tests. Scores at the top cluster closely, public repositories raise contamination risk, and harness and scaffolding choices move results as much as the model does. Treat a few points of difference as noise and newer, harder variants as more informative than saturated ones.

Carlini's C compiler post is a useful corrective: the agents passed huge test suites, yet new features often broke old ones and the code was well below expert quality. Passing tests did not mean done.

1. Pick 10 to 20 recently closed tickets of different types from your own repos, with the merged fix as reference.
  2. Give each tool the same ticket text, the same instruction file and the same check commands.
  3. Score passing checks, reviewer minutes to reach mergeable, rework needed, cost, and any policy violation such as touching tests or unrelated files.
  4. Repeat after major model releases, since rankings shift.
Synthesis: For a BI team, include a dbt model change with data tests, a SQL performance fix with an explain-plan check, and a dashboard change verified by screenshot.

Trap: Reading a 50% time horizon as "can do a 14-hour job." It means a coin-flip success rate on clean, well-specified tasks.
Trap: Judging tools on demos. Your messy legacy repo and review standards are the real benchmark.

cards.q: What does METR's 50% time horizon measure?
cards.a: The length of task, in skilled-human time, that a model completes successfully half the time.

cards.q: What doubling time did METR's fitted trend show for time horizons as of early 2026?
cards.a: About 123 days, roughly every four months.

cards.q: Why does METR caution that time-horizon results overstate real-job readiness?
cards.a: The tasks are well-specified and self-contained, and performance drops substantially under holistic grading.

cards.q: Name three metrics to score in an internal agent evaluation.
cards.a: Passing checks, reviewer minutes to reach a mergeable state, rework needed (also cost and policy violations).

concepts.s: One school of top practitioners treats agents as powerful but fallible collaborators and keeps the engineer responsible for design, tests and review, trading some speed for code they understand.

x.b:
• Agentic Engineering Patterns guide (February 2026), with chapters such as "Writing code is cheap now" and red/green TDD; he defines agentic engineering as professionals amplifying expertise with agents that write and run code.
  • Coined "prompt injection" and the lethal trifecta; advises living dangerously only inside a sandbox.
  • Parallel agents for research, explanations, chores and specified work, with review as the hard limit.

• Beck: "augmented coding", where "you care about the code, its complexity, the tests, & their coverage," versus vibe coding where you care only about behavior. TDD system prompt, structural and behavioral changes in separate commits, and three warning signs (loops, unrequested features, cheating on tests).
  • Ronacher ("A Year Of Vibes", December 2025): works almost entirely through agents as an engineering lead, still reviews heavily, prefers simple code and fewer dependencies, finds MCP does not work for him, and argues failed attempts carry value and review should live in version control.

His February 2026 adoption journey is the clearest on-ramp: drop the chatbot for an agent; reproduce your own work; start end-of-day agents; outsource the slam dunks; engineer the harness; aim to always have an agent running. He is candid that for a long stretch agents felt no faster than doing the work himself, and that his always-on goal is still aspirational.

• Karpathy (X posts, early 2026): the 80/20 flip to agent-driven coding, "mostly programming in English now", a catalogue of model failure modes, watch output "like a hawk" on code that matters, and a predicted 2026 "slopacolypse" of almost-right content.
  • Reed: the spec, plan, todo pipeline with one-question-at-a-time interviews, and a warning about getting "over my skis."

Synthesis: This school converges on: specs and tests written or approved by a human, small reviewable diffs, heavy use of agents for research and chores, sandboxes for autonomy, and continuous harness improvement. Its cost is a review ceiling on throughput, which it accepts in exchange for understanding the codebase.

cards.q: How does Kent Beck distinguish augmented coding from vibe coding?
cards.a: In augmented coding you care about the code, its complexity, the tests and coverage; in vibe coding you care only about the system's behavior.

cards.q: Name Hashimoto's six adoption steps.
cards.a: Drop the chatbot, reproduce your own work, end-of-day agents, outsource the slam dunks, engineer the harness, always have an agent running.

cards.q: What does Ronacher think code review needs to become?
cards.a: Part of the version control system, with prompts and failed attempts visible to teammates.

cards.q: What is Karpathy's predicted 2026 slopacolypse?
cards.a: A flood of low-quality, almost-right AI-generated content across code repositories, papers and social media.

concepts.s: A second school pushes autonomy and parallelism as far as current models allow, reading less code and investing in loops, orchestration and verification instead, with results that are impressive and openly contested.

x.b:
• The Ralph loop: one prompt file, an infinite bash loop, specs and a fix plan on disk, tests as backpressure.
  • "Deterministically bad in an undeterministic world": failures are predictable, so you tune the prompt instead of babysitting each step.
  • Earlier "stdlib" work on building libraries of reusable rules.

Yegge released Gas Town, an open-source orchestrator for many Claude Code or Codex agents, on January 1, 2026. Roles include a Mayor that decomposes work into tasks stored in his Beads tracker, short-lived worker agents each in its own git worktree, a Refinery that merges and checks output, and watchdog agents that restart stuck ones. In a March 2026 conversation with Tim O'Reilly he urged developers to stop reading code ("Code is a liquid").

Maggie Appleton's January 2026 analysis treats Gas Town as design fiction: valuable patterns (persistent roles with disposable sessions, continuous work queues, merge management) wrapped in an ad hoc design, with agents that stall, forget and duplicate work, and costs she estimates at $2,000 to $5,000 a month.

• Steinberger ("Shipping at Inference-Speed", December 2025): mostly Codex, 3 to 8 projects in parallel, commits to main, rarely reads code, and "the amount of software I can create is now mostly limited by inference time." He joined OpenAI in February 2026.
  • Cherny: about five local plus 5 to 10 web sessions, Opus with thinking for all coding, plan first, shared CLAUDE.md, slash commands, a formatting hook, and verification as the top tip. He almost never skips permissions outside a sandbox.

• DORA 2025 links AI adoption to higher throughput and higher instability at the same time.
  • Karpathy's failure catalogue (wrong assumptions, bloat, dead code) is exactly what goes unseen when nobody reads the code.
  • Carlini's compiler shows verified autonomy at scale, and also new features breaking old ones and below-expert code.
Synthesis: The maximalist approach works best where verification is strong and the cost of a defect is low: greenfield tools, prototypes, personal software and well-tested libraries. In regulated systems the same techniques apply, but with humans owning specs, tests and merge.

cards.q: What is Gas Town?
cards.a: Steve Yegge's open-source orchestrator that runs many coding agents in parallel with specialized roles, worker agents in separate worktrees, and a Beads task tracker.

cards.q: What does Steinberger say now limits how much software he can create?
cards.a: Mostly inference time.

cards.q: What is Huntley's tagline for Ralph's failure behavior?
cards.a: Deterministically bad in an undeterministic world, meaning failures are predictable and fixable by tuning the prompt.

cards.q: What monthly cost range did Appleton estimate for Yegge's Gas Town usage?
cards.a: About $2,000 to $5,000 a month.

concepts.s: Agents are moving toward longer autonomous runs, teams of specialized agents and asynchronous cloud execution, which shifts the human bottleneck toward specification, verification design and review.

x.b:
• METR's time-horizon trend has doubled roughly every four months, though on clean tasks.
  • Anthropic's harness posts report multi-hour autonomous app builds, and harnesses getting simpler as Opus 4.5 and 4.6 removed the need for context resets and sprints.
  • Products now ship the pieces: goal conditions, background agent views, scheduled automations and cloud sessions that keep running after you close your laptop.

• Appleton: when agents write the code, design becomes the limiting factor.
  • Willison: review capacity caps how much parallel output is useful.
  • Anthropic's internal study: engineers keep high-level design and taste decisions and delegate work that is easy to verify.
Synthesis: The scarce skills are becoming: writing specs an agent can execute, designing verifiers that catch what matters, decomposing work into independent units, and reviewing fast without losing judgment. These map closely onto senior and staff engineering skills, which is why experienced engineers tend to get more from agents.

• Security: the Clinejection incident shows agents in CI are already being attacked through prompt injection.
  • Quality and stability: DORA's throughput-with-instability finding and Karpathy's slopacolypse warning.
  • Skills: Anthropic's trial on learning, and practitioner reports of atrophy.
  • Measurement: METR could no longer run a clean control group, so evidence will lag practice.

Synthesis: A practical 12-month progression: (1) master the single-session loop with verification on every task; (2) build a shared instruction file, three or four skills and one hook for your team; (3) run two or three parallel sessions in worktrees with a WIP limit; (4) build one long-running harness with a progress file and evaluator for a well-tested side project; (5) put a least-privilege agent into CI for triage or review. Re-read your harness after every major model release and delete what is no longer load-bearing.

cards.q: According to Appleton, what becomes the limiting factor when agents write the code?
cards.a: Design: deciding what to build and how it should work.

cards.q: What types of work did Anthropic engineers report delegating most readily?
cards.a: Work that is easy to verify, low-stakes, repetitive or outside their own context, while keeping high-level design and taste decisions.

cards.q: Why does evidence on agent productivity lag practice?
cards.a: Adoption is so widespread that clean control groups are disappearing, as METR found in 2026.

cards.q: What should you do to your harness after a major model release?
cards.a: Re-examine it and remove components that are no longer load-bearing, adding new ones only where the new model has headroom.
